strengths: Timely and well-motivated work addressing the computational bottleneck of generative classifiers, specifically by exploiting visual autoregressive (VAR) models with tractable likelihoods instead of expensive diffusion ELBO evaluations.

The proposed partial-scale candidate pruning is a natural, elegant fit for the hierarchical coarse-to-fine structure of VAR, achieving substantial computational savings (89x reduction in GFLOPs compared to DiT-based diffusion classifiers with under 1% drop in top-1 accuracy).

Insightful and nuanced findings regarding robustness: the paper demonstrates that the notable out-of-distribution robustness observed in diffusion classifiers does not universally transfer to VAR-based generative classifiers, suggesting that such robustness stems from the denoising diffusion training objective rather than generative classification in general.

The formulation of Token-wise Mutual Information (TMI) provides an intuitive, tractable, and computationally lightweight attribution method for visual explainability, supported by quantitative insertion/deletion evaluation.
The paper is clearly structured and well-written, with thorough ablation studies on likelihood smoothing parameters, variance, and pruning strategies.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100 (with further subsampling of 10 samples per class on distribution-shift datasets). While understandable given the computational demands of generative classifiers, 4,649 GFLOPs per image remains significantly higher than discriminative backbones (e.g., 4.1 GFLOPs for ResNet-50, 16.9 for ViT-B/16), and demonstrating feasibility on full ImageNet-1k would substantially strengthen the claims.

A concerning negative scaling trend is observed in Appendix D (Table 7): as the VAR backbone scales up and generative quality improves (d16 to d30), classification accuracy degrades significantly (from 88.68% down to 71.64% even with CCA), indicating a fundamental unresolved limitation in preserving class-conditional signals as model capacity grows.

The class-incremental learning evaluation is limited in scale (only 10 classes split into two tasks of 5 classes). Evaluating on standard CIL benchmarks (such as Split ImageNet-100 across 5 or 10 sequential tasks) would provide more compelling evidence of applicability.

The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as CCA finetuning is adopted directly from Chen et al. (2024b), and the core components combine existing concepts (coarse-to-fine pruning and Gaussian smoothing) applied to the VAR framework.

strengths: Timely and clear motivation: While recent literature on generative classifiers has almost exclusively focused on diffusion models (which suffer from prohibitive computational costs due to Monte Carlo ELBO approximations), this paper investigates visual autoregressive (VAR) models with tractable likelihoods.

Well-tailored design: Leveraging the coarse-to-fine multi-scale structure of VAR models for partial-scale candidate pruning is an elegant, well-motivated strategy that drastically cuts computation by evaluating only low-resolution token maps in early pruning stages.

Nuanced and honest empirical findings: The paper provides valuable insights by revealing that the out-of-distribution robustness (notably on sketches) observed in diffusion classifiers does not simply generalize to all generative classifiers, pinpointing that such robustness likely stems from the denoising training paradigm rather than generative modeling per se.

Visual explainability via tractable likelihood: The formulation of token-wise mutual information (TMI) enables efficient and faithful visual and contrastive explanations with clear quantitative gains under insertion and deletion metrics compared to black-box explainers like LIME and SHAP.
Clear organization, reproducible details, and thorough ablation studies on smoothing variance, number of samples, and stage configurations.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Adapting conditional likelihoods for classification via Bayes' rule is standard. Candidate pruning is directly adapted from prior diffusion classifier literature (Li et al., 2023), Condition Contrastive Alignment (CCA) is adopted directly from Chen et al. (2024b), and likelihood smoothing is standard Gaussian perturbation.

Evaluation scale is restricted: Main experiments are conducted primarily on ImageNet-100 with subsampled evaluation sets (10 samples per class for distribution-shift datasets). Testing on full ImageNet-1K is missing, which is critical to demonstrate whether the candidate pruning strategy truly scales to thousand-class problems.

Persistent efficiency and accuracy gap with discriminative models: Even with an 89x speedup over diffusion classifiers, A-VARC+ requires ~4,649 GFLOPs per image (compared to ~4.1 GFLOPs for ResNet-50 and ~16.9 GFLOPs for ViT-B/16) while trailing discriminative models in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.

Toy-scale class-incremental evaluation: The class-incremental learning demonstration is evaluated on only 10 classes divided into two tasks (5 classes each), which is too small to substantiate practical utility in real continual learning scenarios.

Scalability inverse scaling issue: As revealed in Appendix Table 7, larger VAR architectures (d16 to d30) exhibit lower classification accuracy (dropping from 83.3% to 64.96%), indicating a fundamental issue with class conditional information dilution as generative fidelity increases.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated study: Generative classifiers have gained significant attention through diffusion models, but their computational complexity remains a major barrier. Leveraging visual autoregressive (VAR) models with tractable likelihoods provides a promising and computationally viable alternative.

Effective architectural adaptations: The proposed techniques—likelihood smoothing to combat codebook quantization instability and partial-scale candidate pruning leveraging the coarse-to-fine hierarchy of VAR—are well-designed and achieve an 89× reduction in computation compared to DiT-based diffusion classifiers with minimal accuracy drop on ImageNet-100.

Insightful and honest empirical findings: The paper provides critical clarity regarding generative classifiers. Specifically, it reveals that the sketch/distribution-shift robustness previously attributed to generative classifiers in diffusion literature stems largely from diffusion denoising dynamics rather than the generative classification framework itself.

Principled visual explainability: Token-wise Mutual Information (TMI) cleanly exploits the exact conditional likelihood factorization of VAR, yielding meaningful, fast, and contrastive visual explanations that quantitatively outperform LIME and SHAP under the proposed setup.

Detailed analysis of the generative vs. discriminative trade-off: The discussion and ablation in Appendix D regarding how larger VAR models dilute class-conditional information with strong structural prediction provide valuable insights for future research in generative classification.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is restricted: Experiments are primarily conducted on ImageNet-100 with only 50 images per class for in-domain evaluation and 10 images per class on out-of-distribution benchmarks. Evaluating on the full ImageNet-1k dataset would make the empirical claims regarding scalability and general applicability substantially stronger.

Incremental nature of core components: While well-integrated, several components are direct adaptations of existing techniques (e.g., Condition Contrastive Alignment is taken directly from Chen et al., 2024b; multi-stage candidate filtering builds on Li et al., 2023).

Limited class-incremental learning benchmark: The class-incremental evaluation in Section 6.2 is conducted on a small toy setup (only 10 classes split into two tasks of 5 classes). Testing on standard continual learning benchmarks (such as Split ImageNet-100 or Split CIFAR-100 across 5–10 steps) is necessary to rigorously validate the practical utility of generative classifiers in incremental settings.

Substantial remaining gap to discriminative baselines: While A-VARC+ closes the gap to diffusion-based generative classifiers, standard discriminative classifiers (ResNets and ViTs) remain vastly superior in both classification accuracy and computational cost (GFLOPs) across almost all tested distributions.

strengths: Compelling motivation and significant efficiency improvements: Generative classifiers based on diffusion models are prohibitively slow due to Monte Carlo ELBO approximations. By leveraging visual autoregressive (VAR) models with tractable likelihoods, the proposed A-VARC+ achieves a ~160x speed-up over DiT-based diffusion classifiers with comparable accuracy on ImageNet-100.

Well-tailored design choices: The proposed partial-scale candidate pruning smartly takes advantage of VAR's hierarchical multi-scale structure (coarse scales require only ~8% of tokens to discard unlikely classes), and latent feature likelihood smoothing effectively mitigates vector quantization fragility.

Nuanced and honest empirical analysis of generative classifier properties: The paper provides a clear and controlled comparison showing that the high out-of-distribution robustness previously attributed to generative classifiers (e.g., on ImageNet-Sketch) is likely an artifact of diffusion denoising objectives rather than an intrinsic property of generative classification in general.

Interesting emergent properties: The exact token-level likelihood allows clean, computationally lightweight visual explanations via token-wise Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI), and class-conditional independence offers natural resistance to catastrophic forgetting in incremental learning.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: Experiments are restricted to ImageNet-100 (and subsampled to 10 images per class for OOD evaluation). Given that a core claim of this paper is computational efficiency, evaluating on the standard full ImageNet-1k benchmark or full OOD test splits would make the empirical validation significantly more convincing.

Inverse scaling behavior with model size: As shown in Appendix Table 4, classification accuracy degrades drastically as the VAR model grows larger (dropping from 83.3% at d16 to 64.96% at d30, or 88.68% to 71.64% with CCA). Although the authors analyze this dilution phenomenon honestly, it reveals a fundamental limitation of scaling autoregressive generative classifiers.

Scale of incremental learning experiments: The class-incremental learning evaluation is demonstrated only as a toy proof-of-concept on 10 classes split into two 5-class tasks, which is too small to substantiate practical continual learning utility.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: Several key building blocks are adapted directly from existing work (such as the CCA finetuning objective from Chen et al., 2024b, and the two-stage candidate pruning paradigm from Li et al., 2023).

strengths: Exploration of a timely and under-studied topic: Adapting visual autoregressive (VAR) models into generative classifiers offers a fresh and valuable alternative to recent diffusion-centric studies.

Well-motivated efficiency enhancements: The partial-scale candidate pruning technique cleverly exploits the multi-scale, coarse-to-fine nature of VAR models to prune candidate classes early, achieving a ~160x speed-up over diffusion classifiers while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Honest scientific analysis and negative results: The authors provide a candid and rigorous comparison showing that VAR classifiers do not inherit the out-of-distribution robustness (e.g., on ImageNet-Sketch) seen in diffusion models, effectively demonstrating that such robustness stems from the denoising objective rather than the generative classification framing itself.

Principled explainability via tractable likelihood: Leveraging token-wise pointwise mutual information (PMI) enables faithful visual and contrastive explanations with minimal computational overhead (requiring only two forward passes).

Insightful analysis of generative vs. discriminative scaling: Appendix C and Table 4 offer a valuable discussion on how larger generative models suffer from class-information dilution as generative fidelity improves.
weaknesses: Restricted evaluation scale: Experiments are conducted predominantly on ImageNet-100 using subsampled evaluation sets (50 images per class for ImageNet-100, and only 10 images per class for distribution-shift benchmarks). Given that one of the main selling points is efficiency, evaluating on the standard full validation sets would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Proof-of-concept class-incremental learning: The continual learning evaluation (Section 6.2) is limited to a toy setup of only 10 classes split into two tasks (5 vs. 5). Comparing against standard continual learning benchmarks (e.g., Split CIFAR-100 or 10-step ImageNet-100) with contemporary continual learning baselines is needed to validate this claim.

Qualitative interpretability without quantitative validation: While the token-wise PMI visualizations in Figures 3, 5, 6, and 7 are visually intuitive, the paper lacks quantitative interpretability evaluations (e.g., pointing game, attribution sanity checks, or faithfulness metrics such as insertion/deletion scores).

Modest methodological novelty: Likelihood smoothing via continuous feature perturbation is conceptually straightforward, and CCA fine-tuning is an existing technique borrowed directly from Chen et al. (2024b). The primary algorithmic contribution is the multi-scale candidate pruning heuristic.

strengths: Exploration of a timely and relevant topic: While generative classifiers have recently seen renewed interest via diffusion models, their prohibitive computational overhead has remained a critical bottleneck. Investigating visual autoregressive (VAR) models provides a fresh perspective and substantially reduces inference runtime.

Honest empirical reporting on robustness: Rather than overclaiming, the authors openly report that the out-of-distribution robustness observed in diffusion classifiers does not transfer to VAR models, offering valuable nuanced insight that OOD robustness may be specific to denoising objectives rather than generic to generative classifiers.

Intuitive hierarchical pruning: Exploiting the multi-scale, coarse-to-fine generation structure of VAR for candidate pruning is natural, conceptually sound, and yields significant runtime savings compared to diffusion-based baselines.

Intrinsically tractable explainability: Leveraging token-wise pointwise mutual information (PMI) provides interpretable, localized attribution maps directly from the model's forward likelihood estimates without requiring gradient-based or sampling-based post-hoc explanations.
weaknesses: Severely restricted evaluation scale and statistical rigor: General classification is evaluated only on ImageNet-100 (50 samples per class), and distribution shift benchmarks are evaluated on only 10 samples per class. This aggressive subsampling introduces substantial estimation variance and weakens the empirical reliability of the benchmark comparisons.

Trivial and under-evaluated class-incremental learning setup: The continual learning evaluation is performed on an extremely small scale (two tasks of 5 classes from ImageNet). Moreover, training separate, independent density estimators for distinct subsets of classes is a trivial and well-known property of generative models (as already explored by Van de Ven et al., 2021), offering minimal methodological novelty here.

Unfavorable scaling behavior: As revealed in Appendix C (Table 4), scaling up the VAR architecture from d16 to d30 results in a severe drop in classification accuracy (from 88.68% down to 71.64% with CCA, and 83.30% to 64.96% without). The fact that stronger generative models exhibit worse discriminative performance highlights a fundamental limitation that impairs the practical viability of scaling this approach.

Heavy reliance on prior finetuning techniques: The core accuracy improvements in A-VARC+ depend heavily on Condition Contrastive Alignment (CCA), an existing finetuning technique introduced by Chen et al. (2024b), limiting the algorithmic novelty of the proposed framework.

Persistent performance gap relative to discriminative baselines: Despite the speedup over diffusion models, A-VARC+ remains noticeably inferior to standard discriminative models (e.g., standard ResNets and ViTs) across almost all benchmark datasets, both in-distribution and out-of-distribution.
